sections.h2: Start with the resale certificate of occupancy
sections.html:
Every sale in South Brunswick, whether you list with an agent, sell privately or accept an as-is cash offer, meets the same township step: a Residential Resale Certificate of Occupancy, issued before the deed changes hands. The township will not release it while any permit or inspection is still open, so sort out your permit history before anything else.

A direct sale gives up some price for speed and usually skips repair negotiations. A listing reaches the most buyers, but it adds commissions, showings and a township inspection to schedule around the sale.

Under section 22-425 of the township code, the certificate rests on a general inspection of the visible parts of the dwelling. The application confirms three things: no work was done that needed a construction or zoning permit, no permits or inspections remain outstanding, and no visible violations or unsafe conditions exist. If an inspector finds a problem, you must obtain the missing permits and satisfy the inspections before the certificate is released.

Residential Resale Certificate of Occupancy at a glance
Certificate detailTownship rule
Code sectionChapter 22, section 22-425
Validity120 days, with one extension of up to 30 days
If the home does not sell in timeWritten application for a new certificate
Fee$125 for a condo, townhome or mobile home; $150 for a single-family dwelling
PickupNot issued in the field; call the Planning office the day after the inspection passes
ContactZoning, 732-329-4000 ext. 7240

Fees can change, so confirm the amount when you apply.

sections.h2: Past projects to check before you book
sections.html:
The application asks whether the home has had any of the following, and for the permit number if so. Anything done without a permit has to be permitted and inspected before the certificate can issue, even if a previous owner did the work.

  • Replacement central air conditioning, furnace or water heater
  • Generator or radon system
  • Addition or finished basement
  • Fireplace or wood stove
  • Shed larger than 200 square feet
  • Swimming pool, hot tub, deck or gazebo

The Building Department administers the state Uniform Construction Code and handles permits, but resale certificates go through the Zoning office. Permits and certificates of approval that come out of the process are passed to the Tax Assessor, so new work will show on the property record.

sections.h2: Why many homes here have replaced systems
sections.html:
South Brunswick grew fast after World War II and again after 1980, so many houses are old enough that a furnace, water heater or central air unit has been replaced at least once. The resale form asks about each replacement, so keep invoices and permit numbers together before you apply.

The township is a set of unincorporated villages, each with its own mail address, and buyers often search by village name. Dayton uses 08810, Kendall Park 08824, Monmouth Junction 08852 and Kingston 08528. Name the village clearly in your listing and on the application. Buyers who search by village will otherwise miss it.

sections.h2: When the inspector finds a problem
sections.html:
The inspection is visual, so it looks at what can be seen without opening walls. When something shows up, the process is simple but it takes time. You obtain the missing permits, satisfy the inspections that go with them, and then the certificate is released. Work that a previous owner did counts as yours once you hold the deed.

Ask these questions before you list. Was the finished basement permitted? Does the shed fit within the 200 square feet allowed without a permit? Did a contractor pull a permit for the water heater, or did a handyman swap it? A yes to any of these needs a permit number in hand when you apply.

If the cost of legalizing old work is high, talk to your attorney about whether the contract should shift that cost to the buyer. Some cash buyers will price the work into their offer and take the repair list off your hands, though the township still wants the permits satisfied before the certificate goes out. Ask each buyer how they plan to handle that step and who will pay the permit fees, so no one is surprised in the last week.

The township has an estimated 47,454 residents in July 2025 and 16,770 households. Of those, 76.9 percent own their home, and the average household has 2.81 people. The middle value of an owner-occupied home is $582,700, median household income is $150,933 and median gross rent is $1,935.

About 52.7 percent of people age five and over speak a language other than English at home. Sellers who advertise in more than one language, or who hand buyers a floor plan and an inspection summary ahead of a tour, tend to avoid repeat questions.

The Kingston Mill Historic District covers 49 acres around the village of Kingston, where South Brunswick meets Princeton and Franklin Township. It includes the 1888 Kingston Mill and the 1798 Kingston Bridge. If you own an older Kingston house, ask the township Planning office whether your address lies inside the district before you plan exterior changes ahead of a sale.

New Jersey puts the Realty Transfer Fee on the seller, collected at recording and scaled to the price stated in the deed. A deed that claims an exemption, such as a transfer between spouses or between parent and child, needs Form RTF-1. For Class 2 residential sales above $1,000,000, a supplemental graduated fee starts at 1% of the total price.

The seller also signs a Gross Income Tax residency form, GIT/REP-3 for New Jersey residents. A nonresident seller prepays at least 2% of the total consideration unless a stated exception applies. Your closing attorney or title agent will prepare the forms.

Work backward from the closing date.

  1. Pull permit numbers and invoices for any replaced systems, additions, sheds or decks.
  2. Call the Zoning office and schedule the inspection.
  3. Fix any violation the inspector lists and ask for a recheck.
  4. Call the Planning office the day after the inspection passes to pick up the certificate.
  5. Check the validity window. If the sale drags past 120 days and an extension, a new application is needed.

A buyer paying cash can close inside that window without trouble. The window matters more for a listing that sits on the market. Keep a copy of the certificate in your closing folder.

faqs.q: Is a township inspection required before closing in South Brunswick?
faqs.a: Yes. South Brunswick requires a Residential Resale Certificate of Occupancy under section 22-425 of the township code. The inspection looks at visible components and checks for unpermitted work, open permits and unsafe conditions.

faqs.q: How long does the South Brunswick resale certificate last?
faqs.a: It is effective for 120 days, and the inspecting officer may grant one extension of up to 30 days. If the house has not sold by then and is still on the market, the owner must apply again.

faqs.q: Which township office handles resale certificates?
faqs.a: The Zoning office does, at 732-329-4000 ext. 7240. The Building Department handles construction permits and new construction certificates, and sends resale questions to Zoning.

faqs.q: Can I sell with work that was done without a permit?
faqs.a: The township wants the permits and inspections satisfied before it issues the resale certificate, so unpermitted work has to be brought into compliance first. Ask your attorney how the sale contract should address any cost of doing so.

faqs.q: Who pays the New Jersey realty transfer fee in South Brunswick?
faqs.a: The seller does. The state collects it at recording, and the rate rises with the price in the deed. Sales above $1,000,000 also carry the graduated percent fee, starting at 1%.
